role: The second reading: each entry read to refute it, not to admire it.
method: Each fragment read whole beside what show.cjs prints for the grape (GRAPES and GRAPES_PLUS, TASTE, INTRO_GRAPES, GRID_SAY, GRID_READS, the service rows) and beside the Codex's region records for the Rhône, Provence and the Languedoc, Jumilla, Navarra and Priorat, Puglia and Sardinia, Curicó and Maule, California, the Barossa, McLaren Vale and Rutherglen, the Swartland, Stellenbosch and Hawke's Bay, with the service reference, the pairing data, the techniques record and codex57's drill filter.

Every fact the reviewed records do not already state was put to search: Shiraz in the Busby cuttings and the earlier shipment argued, the Barossa's turn from American to French oak, the origin of Garnacha and its spread under the Crown of Aragon, the Bandol rule for red and rosé and its months in wood, the VIGNO rules, Durif and Peloursin and the years of 1880, 1884 and 1908, and California's earlier picked Zinfandel.

The glass read as a blind taster would: each note asked whether a taster would nod, each prose field scanned by a script for a family word in disguise, each ladder set beside the Court's grid and the Codex's own climate line for the place, and each tell checked against both entries' notes, so that no tell parts two grapes by a note both carry.

Five contrast grapes and one home grape: each side read for a false or lazy generalisation and for its hedge, each blur for the cool or savoury New World and the warm or modern Old World it must admit, each call for whether it would survive a flight, and each against TASTE.world (both for Syrah, old for Grenache, Mourvèdre and Carignan, new for Zinfandel, none for Petite Sirah) and the Codex's region records for the places it names.

The four lines counted and said aloud for the five beats in order; the sale read for its two sentences and for whether it is said to a guest; the cards and questions read for one key, four options of one kind and a stem that gives nothing away; the notIn lists read against codex57's filter and the bank.

Two rounds of edits, the first pushed as ee2c826 and the second with this record, each an exact replacement in the fragment's own text. node .scripts/grapes/build-grapes.cjs --lint --chunk g9 run after each until it printed six of six sound. The writing build was never run and no file but the six fragments and this record was touched.
limits: This session reached search alone. One source host was tried (wineaustralia.com) and did not resolve, so no further host was tried: a page is cited as search results quoted it, and every address the authors gave stays unconfirmed.

The brief allows five searches a grape. Syrah took two, Grenache one, Mourvèdre one, Carignan one, Petite Sirah one and Zinfandel one; much of each entry stands on the Codex's own reviewed records, which need no new source.

Trade pages whose addresses or titles name a person (a critic's site, a writer's blog, a producer's own history) were read for the fact and are not cited; the fact is cited from another page or from the Codex.

syrah.verdict: Sound after eleven fixes in one round. One grape under two names, the Viognier of Côte-Rôtie, Cornas alone, the white grapes of red Hermitage, the Busby cuttings landed in 1832 and the Barossa vines of the 1840s were confirmed; the Swartland stood on the ripe Shiraz side and the warm rung though the Codex reads its Syrah peppery and savoury, Hawke's Bay stood on the New World side and in the blur at once, the spoken line made every Syrah full bodied, and three tells parted Syrah from its neighbours by notes both carry.
tested: say against GRID_SAY (see-RAH): it opens on it; shih-RAZ is the Codex's Australia record's shi-RAZ, the same sound.
Parentage: Dureza and Mondeuse Blanche, as the reviewed records hold; the year is given as 1998 for the work and 1999 or 2000 for the paper, so the guest answer and the card now say the late 1990s.

Australia: Wine Australia gives Shiraz among Busby's cuttings of 1832, and the Codex's Australia record has them collected in 1831 and landed in 1832; one trade page argues for an earlier shipment in 1817. The 1840s vines stand on the Codex (phylloxera's absence lets them survive) and on Wine Australia's 1843 and 1847.
Oak: Decanter and two trade pages give American oak as the long Barossa custom, a turn to French oak and less new wood, and some return to American oak for cost.

The glass as a blind taster: every note set beside the reviewed profile and the Court's two grid reads; blackberry, blueberry, pepper, olive, smoked meat and violet all nod. A script scanned every prose field for a family word in disguise and found none.

Old World and New World against TASTE.world (both) and the Codex's own region records: the Swartland read peppery, savoury and firm but not heavy, Stellenbosch riper, Hawke's Bay and the Yarra near the northern Rhône, Washington dark, peppery and meaty, the Barossa floor rich, chocolatey and high in alcohol. The ladder agrees with the grid: the northern Rhône moderate, Australia warm.
Côte-Rôtie up to 20 per cent Viognier, Cornas all Syrah and Marsanne and Roussanne in red Hermitage, against the Codex's Rhône record: agree.
Service against the full tannic reds row, which names Syrah, the decanting row, which names Syrah, and TASTE.age (five to twenty): agree.
The four lines counted and said aloud: five beats in order, the sale two sentences, a hook and a pour.
Compare tells read from both sides against the Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Petit Verdot, Pinotage, Blaufränkisch, Mourvèdre, Zinfandel and Petite Sirah entries.
Cards and questions: one key each, four options of one kind, nothing given away, the worlds question first.
open: Lavender beside violet stands on tasting notes, as the author flagged; a blind taster may nod at violet alone. Left.
The author's report still names Hawke's Bay and the Swartland on the New World side; the report is not shipped and the fields now read otherwise.

changed.was: Syrah and Shiraz are one grape under two names. Its home is the northern Rhône, on the steep river slopes of Hermitage and Côte-Rôtie. It is deep purple and tastes of blackberry, blueberry and cracked black pepper, often with a savoury note of black olive or smoked meat. It is full bodied, with firm tannin, and aged in oak. The Rhône tends to be peppery and savoury, while Australian Shiraz is typically riper and richer, with chocolate and vanilla. Pour it with grilled lamb, venison or a peppered steak. Australia has grown it since 1832, and the Barossa still picks from vines planted in the 1840s.
changed.now: Syrah and Shiraz are one grape under two names. Its home is the northern Rhône, on the steep river slopes of Hermitage and Côte-Rôtie. It is deep purple and tastes of blackberry, blueberry and cracked black pepper, often with a savoury note of black olive or smoked meat. It is medium to full bodied, with firm tannin, and usually aged in oak. The Rhône tends to be peppery and savoury, while Australian Shiraz is typically riper and richer, with chocolate and vanilla. Pour it with grilled lamb, venison or a peppered steak. Australia has grown it since 1832, and the Barossa still picks from vines planted in the 1840s.
changed.why: The line made every Syrah full bodied, where the reviewed profile and the entry's own structure read the Rhône medium plus and the Barossa full; aged in oak was said of every bottle, so usually hedges it. Three words in all.

grenache.verdict: Sound after thirteen fixes over two rounds. Châteauneuf-du-Pape's thirteen grapes, Tavel rosé only, Banyuls, Cannonau and an origin in Aragon spread under its Crown to Sardinia and Roussillon were confirmed; the twenty dropped the hedge on the origin the rest keeps, the Old World cellar made Garnacha a blend even in Spain, the New World glass kept the sweet, candied style typical where the Codex reads the Barossa and McLaren Vale now perfumed and mid weight, the call leaned on that candied edge, and the drill gathered questions on Garnacha Blanca.

Origin: Wikipedia and Decanter give Aragon as the common view, Sardinia as argued by some, and the spread under the Crown of Aragon to Sardinia in the fourteenth century and to Roussillon.

Service: the medium reds row names Côtes du Rhône; the reference gives Grenache a Burgundy bowl; TASTE.age five to fifteen: agree.

carignan.verdict: Sound after eleven fixes in one round. Mazuelo, Cariñena and Samsó, Carignano del Sulcis, the VIGNO vines of thirty years, head trained, dry farmed and two years before sale, and carbonic maceration in the Languedoc were confirmed; the call, a card and the worlds question parted the Old World from Maule by dried thyme though the Codex reads Maule Carignan of damson and dried herb, the New World cellar put every bottle on dry farmed vines and every Maule bottle under VIGNO, the twenty had old vines turn acidity into fruit, and a label made all Carignano del Sulcis old and ungrafted.
tested: say: kah-reen-YAHN as the Codex's Languedoc and Maule records; Cariñena as the Priorat record writes it. The Lebanon record writes kah-ree-NYAHN, the same sound.

VIGNO: thirty year old, head trained, dry farmed vines of the Maule secano and 24 months before release on trade pages; the share is 65, 70 or 85 per cent by page and 65 in the Codex's Chile record, so no share is given, as the author chose.
Maule's climate: the Codex reads it cooler and wetter than Colchagua, warm days and cool nights, so the moderate rung stands.
Carbonic maceration: the Codex's Languedoc record gives it to Carignan to tame the tannin, and its technique record describes intact berries; fermented whole stands.
The glass against the profile (black raspberry, cranberry, dried cherry, plum, garrigue, iron, liquorice, a meaty savour): every note nods; graphite rests on Priorat's slate. Left.
Old World and New World against TASTE.world (old) and the plan's reason for a side by side; the contrast is one of degree, and the call ends on the high acidity both keep.
Service against the medium reds row and TASTE.age (old vines five to fifteen): agree.
Compare tells read from both sides against the Grenache, Mourvèdre and Cinsault entries.
The four lines counted and said aloud; cards and questions read for one key, four options of one kind, nothing given away.
open: The side by side is the thinnest of the chunk: Maule and the Languedoc differ by degree. The plan fixes contrast and names Maule in its reason; a reviewer may still judge at home and abroad the better form.

changed.was: Carignan is a Mediterranean red that keeps high acidity and firm tannin even in great heat. Old vines in the Languedoc, Spain and Sardinia turn that into black raspberry, cranberry and dried thyme, in a wine made for rich, rustic food.
changed.now: Carignan is a Mediterranean red that keeps high acidity and firm tannin even in great heat. Old vines in the Languedoc, Spain and Sardinia give it depth: black raspberry, cranberry and dried thyme, in a wine made for rich, rustic food.
changed.why: Old vines turn that into black raspberry said that high acidity and tannin become fruit; old vines give it depth, as the guest answer on old vines says.

changed.was: Carignan was long the workhorse of the Languedoc, and it is old hillside vines that have made its name. It tastes of black raspberry, cranberry and dried cherry, with dried thyme and liquorice. It is deep in colour, with high acidity and firm, rustic tannin. Many cellars ferment the berries whole in a sealed vat, which softens that grip. The Languedoc and Spain tend to be savoury, while old vines in Chile and California are often juicier and more openly fruity. Pour it with cassoulet, grilled sausages or lamb. Spain, where it began, calls it Cariñena or Mazuelo, and old vine growers in Chile share one name for theirs, Vigno.
changed.now: Carignan was long the workhorse of the Languedoc, and old hillside vines have made its name. It tastes of black raspberry, cranberry and dried cherry, with dried thyme and liquorice. It is deep in colour, with high acidity and firm, rustic tannin. Many cellars ferment the berries whole in a sealed vat, which softens that grip. changed.why: Where it began wanted the hedge the reference works keep (Aragon is the likely home); three words came out of the first sentence to keep the line at 109.

petite-sirah.verdict: Sound after six fixes in one round. Durif a cross of Peloursin by Syrah, raised in a French nursery about 1880, true Durif in California from 1884, the old California vines proved mostly Durif by DNA at Davis in the late 1990s, and Rutherglen since 1908 were confirmed; the spoken line said neither small beside a guest answer on small berries, three lines said bred where the sources say found and propagated, a guest answer said nearly all where the work found most, and two tells parted the grape from Syrah and Malbec by notes both carry.
tested: say: puh-TEET sih-RAH and DUR-if, as the Codex's California and Rutherglen records.

The profile against the Codex's California record (Durif, the inky, tannic child of Syrah and Peloursin, an old field blend partner of Zinfandel in Sonoma and Lodi) and Rutherglen record (deep, dense, tannic and plummy): agree.

zinfandel.verdict: Sound after two fixes in one round. Primitivo and Tribidrag as one vine, the Vienna nursery and Long Island in the 1820s, the Gold Rush, Manduria and Gioia del Colle, the Dolce Naturale and Old Vine with no legal meaning were confirmed against the Codex's California and Puglia records; the spoken line called Tribidrag the oldest name where the records date its first mention differently, and the blur admitted the Old World's exception but not the New World's.
tested: say: ZIN-fan-del, the Court's; pree-mee-TEE-voh, the Codex's.
History against the Codex's California record: the east coast in the 1820s, Gold Rush Zinfandel in Amador and El Dorado, Old Vine with no legal meaning.

Old World and New World against TASTE.world (new) and the Codex's Puglia record, which reads Primitivo ripe, sweet fruited, inky and jammy, the richest from Manduria and the freshest from Gioia del Colle. The entry's savoury, rustic Primitivo is a lean of degree, and the blur's plush Primitivo admits the rest.
California's earlier picked wines: Decanter and Wine Spectator report cellars picking two to three weeks earlier, with less new oak, since the big vintages of the late 1990s.
Structure: TASTE gives tannin one step, the profile and the grid medium to medium plus; the entry follows the profile and the grid, as the author reported.
The ladder: Gioia del Colle moderate on the Codex's Puglia record (the Murge cools the nights); Dry Creek, Lodi, Amador and Paso Robles warm with the grid.
Service against the full tannic reds row, which names Zinfandel, and TASTE.age (three to eight): agree.
Compare tells read from both sides against the Grenache, Syrah, Corvina profile, Pinotage and Petite Sirah entries.
The four lines counted and said aloud; cards and questions read for one key, four options of one kind, nothing given away.
open: The Codex's Puglia record reads Primitivo inky where the reviewed profile reads Zinfandel medium to deep ruby, rarely opaque; the entry says nothing of Primitivo's colour.

changed.was: Zinfandel reached California in the Gold Rush, and old, gnarled vines still grow in Lodi, Sonoma and the Sierra Foothills. It tastes of blackberry jam, raspberry and black pepper. Its bunches ripen unevenly, which often leaves a raisin edge. The colour is only medium and the tannin moderate, but the alcohol is high. American oak often adds vanilla and a hint of dill. In Puglia, where it is called Primitivo, it tends to be more savoury, with leather and tobacco. It belongs with barbecue: smoky ribs, a spiced sausage or a burger. DNA finally traced it home to Croatia, where its oldest name is Tribidrag.
changed.now: Zinfandel reached California in the Gold Rush, and old, gnarled vines still grow in Lodi, Sonoma and the Sierra Foothills. It tastes of blackberry jam, raspberry and black pepper. Its bunches ripen unevenly, which often leaves a raisin edge. The colour is only medium and the tannin moderate, but the alcohol is high. American oak often adds vanilla and a hint of dill. In Puglia, where it is called Primitivo, it tends to be more savoury, with leather and tobacco. It belongs with barbecue: smoky ribs, a spiced sausage or a burger. DNA finally traced it home to Croatia, where old records call it Tribidrag.
changed.why: Oldest reads as a superlative to the lint, and the records date the first mention of Tribidrag differently (the fifteenth century on one page, 1518 on another); old records call it states the fact without ranking it.

changed.now: Some Puglian cellars pick very ripe and use new oak, for a plush Primitivo hard to tell from California, while some California cellars now pick earlier for fresher wines.
changed.why: The blur admitted only the Old World's exception. Since the big vintages of the late 1990s some California cellars pick two to three weeks earlier, with less new oak, for fresher wines; that is the New World's.

codexRecords: TASTE gives Zinfandel tannin one step (tan 1) where GRAPES reads medium to medium plus, INTRO_GRAPES 2 and the Court's grid medium and medium plus. The table follows GRAPES and the grid. The author's flag, upheld.

The Codex's Puglia record reads Primitivo inky, jammy and sweet fruited, while GRAPES reads Zinfandel medium to deep ruby, rarely opaque. The table keeps only medium colour for Zinfandel, says nothing of Primitivo's colour, and makes its savoury Primitivo a lean of degree with the plush one in the blur.

TASTE.world reads old for Grenache and new for Zinfandel, while the plan fixes both as side by side; the plan's own rule for a side by side suggests both. The author's flag for Zinfandel, extended to Grenache.
The Court's grid reads Châteauneuf-du-Pape's tannin medium to medium plus and GRAPES reads Grenache's low to medium; the grid reads the blend, the profile the grape. The table follows the profile.

The Codex's Provence record says both that sea breezes temper the heat near the coast and that Mourvèdre needs the sea's warmth to ripen at Bandol. The table keeps Bandol on a moderate rung, as the first.

The Codex respells Grenache two ways (gruh-NASH in the grid and the Australia record, gruh-NAHSH in the Rhône record), Monastrell two ways (mo-nas-TREL and mo-nahs-TREL) and Carignan two ways (kah-reen-YAHN, kah-ree-NYAHN in the Lebanon record), each the same sound. The table takes gruh-NASH, mo-nahs-TREL and kah-reen-YAHN.

js/data-intro.js still draws bare family words for these grapes on the old surfaces: Carignan (red and black fruit, dried herb), Mourvèdre (earth, herbs), Grenache (dried herb) and Zinfandel (sweet spice). The table names the thing and leaves those rows as they are.
unsettled: Whether any source address still answers: none could be opened from this session.
Whether Shiraz first reached Australia with Busby's cuttings of 1832 or with an earlier shipment of 1817: the table says 1832 on most accounts on the card and since 1832 in the spoken line.
The year of Syrah's parentage: 1998 for the work, 1999 or 2000 for the paper, by page. The table says the late 1990s.
Whether the eighteen months in wood of Bandol red is in the cahier itself: the Codex and the appellation's brochure state it; the cahier excerpts read did not show it.
The share of Carignan VIGNO asks for: 65, 70 or 85 per cent by page. The table gives none.
Whether Carignan's side by side is wide enough to keep: the plan fixes it; the table writes it as a matter of degree.
Mendocino as a moderate rung for Petite Sirah, and lavender among Syrah's floral notes: on trade notes alone.
settled: Shiraz is the Syrah of Busby's cuttings, collected in 1831 and landed in 1832, and the Barossa still holds vines of the 1840s.

The Swartland's Syrah is peppery and savoury, Stellenbosch's riper; Hawke's Bay and the Yarra read nearer the northern Rhône. The first and the cool sites stand in the blur, not on the ripe Shiraz side.
Barossa Shiraz was long aged in American oak and has turned to French oak and less new wood, with some return to American oak.
Grenache most likely began in Aragon and spread under its Crown to Sardinia and Roussillon; Australia's Grenache is now often perfumed and mid weight.
Bandol red is at least half Mourvèdre and its rosé at least a fifth; the red spends at least eighteen months in wood, by tradition large old casks.
Jumilla Monastrell is ripe with dried fig, earth and game and high tannin, and Australian Mataro dark, meaty and tannic.
Maule Carignan is dark, high in acidity and savoury, of damson and dried herb; VIGNO asks for thirty year old, head trained, dry farmed vines and two years before release.
Durif is Peloursin crossed with Syrah, raised in a French nursery about 1880; true Durif reached California in 1884 and Rutherglen in 1908, and most old California Petite Sirah proved to be Durif.
Some California cellars now pick Zinfandel earlier, with less new oak, for fresher wines.
